triage.name: Asthma in Children
triage.reason: Classic pediatric presentation with recurrent wheeze, cough and dyspnea; diagnosis reachable by history, exam and spirometry, with important look-alikes such as bronchiolitis and foreign body.

demographics: More common in boys during childhood; the pattern reverses after puberty, when asthma becomes more common in girls
Higher prevalence among Black and Puerto Rican children in the US
More common in children living in low-income urban areas

risk_factors.text: Parent with asthma, especially the mother
Personal history of atopic dermatitis or allergic rhinitis
Exposure to secondhand tobacco smoke, including during pregnancy
Frequent viral respiratory infections in early childhood

family_history: Asthma in a parent or sibling
Eczema or hay fever in the family
social_history: Cockroach or mouse infestation in the home
Pets with fur or feathers in the home

chief_complaints.text: My child keeps coughing at night
My child can't keep up when playing

hpi.onset: Symptoms often begin in early childhood, frequently before age 5; individual episodes start over minutes to hours, sometimes after a cold that has been going on for a few days
hpi.duration: Episodes last hours to days; the underlying tendency is chronic, with symptoms that come and go over months to years
hpi.progression: Symptoms wax and wane. Many children have intermittent episodes separated by weeks or months of feeling well, often worse at night and in the early morning. Some have symptoms most days. Attacks can build gradually or come on suddenly after a trigger.
hpi.quality: Whistling or musical sound when breathing out, with a sensation of chest tightness and air hunger
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; children between episodes may feel completely normal, while during an attack they may be unable to speak in full sentences or feed normally
hpi.timing: Often worse at night and in the early morning; frequently triggered by exercise, cold air, or a cold
relieving: Nebulized medicine in the office or emergency department

associated_symptoms.text: Runny or stuffy nose and sneezing
Trouble feeding or sucking in infants

pertinent_negatives: Wheezing that started suddenly while eating or playing with a small object
Wheezing present since birth without symptom-free periods
Frequent spitting up or choking with feeds
Poor weight gain or failure to thrive
Symptoms that only occur with one specific food

negatives: Wheezing that started suddenly while eating or playing with a small toy
Wheezing since birth without any symptom-free periods

argues_against: Chronic sinusitis as the sole cause

positives.text: Spitting up or vomiting with feeds in infants

negatives: Poor feeding with poor weight gain

positives.text: Itchy rash in the creases of the arms and legs

argues_against: Food allergy as the only trigger

positives.text: Known allergies to dust, pets, or pollen

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants cannot describe symptoms; they present with trouble feeding or sucking, rapid breathing, and irritability. Wheezing may be the only sign, and it can be hard to tell apart from bronchiolitis.
missing_classic_features: Nighttime cough described by the child

atypical.how_it_differs: Breathlessness with activity and reduced exercise tolerance are more prominent and may be attributed to weight rather than asthma, delaying diagnosis.
Young children often cannot perform spirometry and may not report chest tightness; parents describe the symptoms instead. A trial of asthma medicine is sometimes used to support the diagnosis.

general.mild: Comfortable, playful, speaking in full sentences; may have mild tachypnea or audible wheeze at rest
general.moderate: Sitting upright, preferring not to lie flat; speaking in short phrases; visibly working to breathe; can feed but tires
general.severe: Tripod or upright posture, cannot speak in full sentences, agitated or drowsy, marked accessory muscle use, audible wheeze
general.critical: Exhausted, confused or lethargic, minimal air movement, may have paradoxical breathing; impending respiratory failure

findings.maneuver: Listen with the stethoscope over the trachea and both lung fields during quiet breathing
findings.finding: Expiratory wheezing, often musical or polyphonic, loudest on expiration

findings.maneuver: Auscultate and time the expiratory phase compared with inspiration
findings.finding: Expiratory phase longer than inspiratory phase

findings.maneuver: Observe the child's breathing for use of neck and intercostal muscles
findings.finding: Suprasternal, supraclavicular, or intercostal retractions; nasal flaring; head bobbing in infants

findings.maneuver: Count the respiratory rate for a full minute while the child is calm
findings.finding: Respiratory rate above the normal range for age

findings.maneuver: Measure oxygen saturation with pulse oximetry on room air

findings.finding: Minimal or absent breath sounds with little wheeze despite severe distress

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips, tongue, and nail beds
Inspect and palpate the chest wall
findings.finding: No focal asymmetry, no localized dullness or decreased breath sounds

findings.maneuver: Listen over the neck and trachea for inspiratory sounds

findings.finding: Normal S1 and S2 without murmur or gallop
Dark infraorbital circles (allergic shiners) and a transverse nasal crease from the allergic salute
Pale, boggy nasal turbinates with clear discharge

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin, especially flexural areas
findings.finding: Dry, itchy, eczematous patches in the antecubital or popliteal fossae

labs.caveat: A modest eosinophilia supports an allergic (atopic) phenotype but is neither sensitive nor specific; a normal value does not argue against asthma.
Usually normal in asthma; a marked elevation points toward pneumonia or another infection rather than asthma.
Mild leukocytosis is uncommon in uncomplicated asthma and should prompt consideration of a concurrent infection.

findings.finding: Right axis deviation or prominent right atrial and right ventricular forces suggesting chronic hypoxemia or pulmonary hypertension

findings.text: Normal or hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms
Peribronchial cuffing or thickened bronchial walls
Patchy atelectasis, especially of the right middle lobe
Hyperlucent lung field with mediastinal shift suggesting a foreign body or pneumothorax

initial.why: Confirms airflow obstruction and reversibility in children old enough to perform the maneuver (usually age 5 and older)
Office or home measurement of peak expiratory flow; useful for monitoring and for older children who can cooperate
Not routine; helps exclude pneumonia, foreign body, or other structural causes
initial.only_if: the presentation is atypical, the first episode is severe, or another diagnosis is suspected

supporting.why: Identifies allergic triggers and supports an atopic phenotype
supporting.only_if: there is a history of allergies or the trigger pattern is unclear

supporting.why: Alternative to skin testing when skin testing is not feasible
supporting.only_if: skin testing is unavailable or not tolerated

supporting.why: A trial of controller therapy with reassessment is often used to support the diagnosis in young children who cannot perform spirometry
supporting.only_if: the child is too young for reliable lung function testing

not_indicated.why: Not needed for a typical asthma presentation; a normal white count does not change management
Not routinely helpful; reserve for concern about bacterial infection
No role in asthma; consider only if bacterial pneumonia is suspected
Not indicated for routine asthma evaluation; reserve for suspected structural or interstitial disease
Not routine for a typical, previously diagnosed asthma exacerbation
not_indicated.only_if: the presentation is atypical, the first episode is severe, or another diagnosis is suspected

decision_points: Spirometry requires a child old enough to perform forced expiratory maneuvers reliably, usually age 5 or older; younger children are diagnosed clinically and by treatment response
A chest x-ray is not routine for a typical exacerbation but should be obtained when the presentation is atypical or a complication is suspected
Consider a trial of controller therapy with reassessment when the diagnosis is uncertain in a young child
Assess for alternative diagnoses such as foreign body aspiration, bronchiolitis, or structural airway lesions when symptoms are atypical

criteria.name: Clinical diagnosis of asthma in children
criteria.summary: Diagnosis is based on a history of recurrent episodes of wheezing, cough, chest tightness, or difficulty breathing, often worse at night or with triggers such as exercise, cold air, allergens, or viral infections, together with evidence of variable expiratory airflow limitation. In children old enough for spirometry, airflow obstruction that improves after a bronchodilator supports the diagnosis. In younger children, a documented response to a trial of asthma therapy can support the diagnosis.

differential.name: Bronchiolitis
differential.why_considered: Wheezing and respiratory distress in a young child, especially during viral season

history: Age under 2 years, most often under 12 months
Symptoms begin with a runny nose and low-grade fever, then cough and wheeze over 1 to 2 days
First episode, no prior recurrent wheeze
labs: Viral testing positive for RSV or another respiratory virus
imaging: Chest x-ray with hyperinflation and perihilar streaking; not routinely needed

differential.name: Foreign body aspiration
differential.why_considered: Sudden wheezing or coughing in a toddler who was playing with small objects
differential.trigger: Abrupt onset of wheeze or cough while eating or playing with a small object, or a focal unilateral wheeze

history: Sudden onset during eating, playing, or laughing
Symptoms may be intermittent and unilateral
exam: Focal decreased breath sounds or unilateral wheeze
Stridor if the object is in the upper airway
imaging: Hyperlucent lung field with air trapping and mediastinal shift on expiratory or decubitus views
Object may be radiolucent and not visible on plain film

differential.name: Pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Cough, tachypnea, and respiratory distress in a febrile child

exam: Focal crackles or dullness to percussion

differential.name: Cystic fibrosis
differential.why_considered: Recurrent wheezing and respiratory symptoms in a young child
differential.trigger: Failure to thrive, chronic productive cough, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, or salty-tasting skin

history: Poor weight gain or failure to thrive despite adequate intake
labs: Elevated sweat chloride on sweat testing
Low fecal elastase if pancreatic insufficiency
imaging: Chest x-ray with bronchiectasis, hyperinflation, or mucus plugging

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux with aspiration
differential.why_considered: Cough and wheeze in an infant, especially around feeds

history: Symptoms worse after feeding or when lying flat
imaging: Upper GI series may show reflux or aspiration

differential.name: Vocal cord dysfunction
differential.why_considered: Episodic breathlessness and noisy breathing in an older child or teen

history: Symptoms occur at rest or with stress, not primarily with exercise
Poor response to asthma controller therapy
Symptoms may be triggered by anxiety or strong emotions
exam: Wheeze loudest over the neck rather than the chest
Normal oxygen saturation during severe symptoms

differential.name: Allergic rhinitis
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough and nasal symptoms in an atopic child

history: Prominent sneezing, itchy eyes, and clear nasal discharge
Symptoms seasonal or with allergen exposure
Cough is postnasal drip related, not wheeze

differential.name: Structural airway lesion
differential.why_considered: Persistent noisy breathing or wheeze in an infant without symptom-free periods

history: Symptoms present since birth or early infancy
May have been intubated or have vascular ring
imaging: Bronchoscopy showing airway compression or malacia
Chest x-ray or CT showing vascular ring

severity.mild: Symptoms less than twice a week, nighttime symptoms less than twice a month, no limitation of activity, FEV1 at or above 80% predicted, exacerbations brief and rare
severity.moderate: Symptoms daily, nighttime symptoms more than once a week, some activity limitation, FEV1 60 to 80% predicted, exacerbations affect activity and sleep
severity.severe: Symptoms throughout the day, nighttime symptoms most nights, marked activity limitation, FEV1 below 60% predicted, frequent exacerbations requiring oral corticosteroids
severity.critical: Life-threatening exacerbation with exhaustion, minimal air movement, silent chest, cyanosis, altered mental status, or impending respiratory failure requiring intensive care

red_flags.finding: Silent chest or minimal air movement despite severe distress
red_flags.meaning: Impending respiratory failure; needs immediate escalation

red_flags.finding: Cyanosis of lips, tongue, or nail beds
red_flags.meaning: Severe hypoxemia; give oxygen and prepare for advanced support

red_flags.finding: Unable to speak in full sentences or feed
Oxygen saturation below 90% on room air
red_flags.meaning: Severe hypoxemia; needs continuous monitoring and aggressive therapy

red_flags.finding: Sudden onset of wheeze while eating or playing with a small object
red_flags.meaning: Foreign body aspiration until proven otherwise

red_flags.finding: Poor weight gain, chronic productive cough, or clubbing
red_flags.meaning: Consider cystic fibrosis or another chronic condition

complications.name: Acute severe exacerbation requiring emergency care or hospitalization
Airway remodeling with persistent airflow limitation
clues: Reduced FEV1 that does not fully reverse

special_populations.differences: Cannot report symptoms; present with feeding difficulty, rapid breathing, and irritability. Wheezing may be the only sign and is hard to distinguish from bronchiolitis. Spirometry is not possible.
Young children often cannot perform spirometry and may not report chest tightness; diagnosis is clinical and may rely on a trial of controller therapy. Boys are more commonly affected before puberty.
Breathlessness with activity and reduced exercise tolerance are more prominent and may be attributed to weight, delaying diagnosis. Response to controller therapy may be reduced.
Adolescent pregnancy may be accompanied by changes in asthma control; some improve and some worsen. Poorly controlled asthma increases risk of preterm birth and low birth weight.

key_questions.question: How often do the wheezing or coughing episodes happen, and how long do they last?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent episodes over weeks to months, not a single continuous illness; frequency and duration help grade severity

key_questions.question: Does your child cough or wheeze at night or early in the morning?
key_questions.looking_for: Nighttime or early morning symptoms, a hallmark of asthma

key_questions.question: What seems to bring it on?
key_questions.looking_for: Exercise, cold air, dust, pets, pollen, smoke, or colds; a clear trigger pattern supports asthma

key_questions.question: Does the breathing medicine (albuterol) help, and how quickly?
key_questions.looking_for: Rapid relief after a bronchodilator supports reversible airflow obstruction

key_questions.question: How many days of school or play has your child missed?
key_questions.looking_for: Missed school or limited activity suggests poor control

key_questions.question: Is there any wheezing or noisy breathing between episodes, or does your child feel completely well?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptom-free intervals favor asthma over structural or chronic disease

key_questions.question: Did the wheezing start suddenly while eating or playing with a small object?
key_questions.looking_for: Abrupt onset with choking suggests foreign body aspiration, not asthma

key_questions.question: Has your child ever had a cough or wheeze that has never gone away since birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Continuous symptoms since birth suggest a structural airway lesion or another chronic disease

key_questions.question: Does your child have eczema, hay fever, or food allergies?
key_questions.looking_for: Atopic history supports an allergic asthma phenotype

key_questions.question: Does anyone in the family have asthma, eczema, or hay fever?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of atopy, especially maternal asthma

key_questions.question: Does anyone smoke in the home or around your child?
key_questions.looking_for: Secondhand smoke exposure, a strong modifiable trigger

key_questions.question: What is the home like - any pets, mold, dampness, cockroaches, or mice?
key_questions.looking_for: Indoor allergens that can be reduced

key_questions.question: Does your child have trouble feeding or sucking, or is he or she tiring during feeds?
key_questions.looking_for: Feeding difficulty in infants suggests significant respiratory distress

key_questions.question: Has your child had any fever, weight loss, night sweats, or poor weight gain?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in typical asthma; present suggests infection, cystic fibrosis, or another diagnosis

key_questions.question: Is your child taking any medicines, including aspirin or ibuprofen?
key_questions.looking_for: Aspirin or NSAID exposure can trigger bronchospasm in some children

reasoning_points: Recurrent episodes of wheezing, cough, chest tightness, or difficulty breathing separated by symptom-free periods
Symptoms worse at night or early morning and provoked by typical triggers such as exercise, cold air, allergens, smoke, or viral infections
Evidence of variable expiratory airflow limitation, such as improvement after a bronchodilator on spirometry or a documented response to a trial of asthma therapy
Atopic history or family history of asthma and allergy supporting the diagnosis
Alternative diagnoses considered and excluded, including foreign body aspiration, bronchiolitis, pneumonia, cystic fibrosis, and structural airway lesions
Severity graded from symptom frequency, nighttime awakenings, activity limitation, and lung function to guide therapy

easy: School-age child with recurrent wheezing episodes and clear symptom-free intervals
Symptoms worse at night and with exercise or cold air
Personal or family history of eczema, allergic rhinitis, or asthma
medium: Preschool child too young for reliable spirometry, diagnosed clinically and by response to a controller trial
Symptoms only with colds, mistaken for recurrent respiratory infections
Wheezing with exercise only, without nighttime symptoms
Coexisting allergic rhinitis or obesity obscuring the picture
hard: Infant with wheezing and feeding difficulty, hard to distinguish from bronchiolitis
Toddler with sudden focal wheeze after playing with a small object (foreign body)
Child with chronic productive cough, poor weight gain, or clubbing suggesting cystic fibrosis
Teenager with episodic breathlessness and noisy breathing that is actually vocal cord dysfunction
Severe exacerbation with a quiet chest, cyanosis, or exhaustion
